newsitem.title: UK: Dropped vowel lands British fraudsters in court.
newsitem.headline: Dropped vowel lands British fraudsters in court.

text.p: Fraudsters were taught a lesson by Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) on Monday -- in spelling.
The office, which investigates and prosecutes serious financial crimes, revealed how a gang had been linked by forged documents which were all signed "yours sincerly" rather than "yours sincerely".
Between December 1995 and May 1996 the major clearing banks were defrauded of almost 2.0 million pounds ($3.4 million), the SFO said in a statement.
The case was wrapped up on Monday when Richard Culverhouse was found guilty at Birmingham Crown Court of obtaining property by deception and attempting to obtain by deception.
Culverhouse was involved in a nation-wide scheme to steal money from the banking system by manipulating the Clearing House Automated Payment System (CHAPS).

"This fraud was alarmingly simple to carry out. Had the defendants succeeded in all of their dishonest efforts the loss would have been over seven million pounds at the time of their activities being stopped," SFO lawyer Phillip Lewis said.

When arrested in March 1996, the five organisers of the fraud -- who all pleaded guilty -- and a group charged by the SFO as "stooge" recipients of the money, were seeking to obtain more than 1.0 million pounds a month, Lewis said.
The frauds were carried out by forging a letter of authority from a customer of one bank and requesting money to be transferred to an account at another.
The idea was for the money to be withdrawn in cash from the second bank and passed on to the organisers before the forgery was discovered, the SFO said.
A percentage of the money was paid to the recipient of the funds for the people who were willing for their accounts to be used to receive funds.
Efforts to make sure the pattern of a major co-ordinated fraud were not recognised meant the fraudsters deliberately spread their efforts around the country, but their spelling gave the game away.
"It was a simple recurring spelling mistake that led the 20 different police forces involved to recognise that a major co-ordinated crime had taken place," the SFO said.
The gang made 131 attempts to transfer money from accounts of various companies, and was successful on 33 occasions. A company's bank details were obtained by pretending they were buying a product.
The conspirators then forged the company in question's letterhead and directors' signatures from public records and use the forged authority to transfer money from its account.
Target firms included travel agencies, builders merchants and finally financial services providers. Names were picked out of the telephone directory.

Culverhouse was one of 10 people charged by the SFO as "stooge" recipients. Seven of his co-defendants pleaded guilty to similar offences. The SFO offered no evidence against an eighth and a warrant is outstanding for the arrest of a ninth.
Five other people were charged as organisers of the fraud, all five pleaded guilty to conspiracy. Sentencing is due to take place on July 24 or 25.

The SFO pointed out that while banks across the country were affected, all the attempts to bring about fraudulent transfers of funds "would have been defeated if the accounts had been password protected". ($ = 0.591 British Pounds)
